issues.legal_issue: The government’s later return of property seized in an act of state constitutes a fresh grant when the seizure extinguished all prior rights, rather than restoring antecedent title.
material_facts: The government seized the ruler’s private and public properties in an exercise of sovereign power.
The Privy Council had held that the seizure covered both private and public properties and that the municipal courts had no jurisdiction to question it.
The government later issued an order relinquishing and restoring the private properties to the ruler’s widows.
The property in dispute derived from the Tanjore Palace Estate, and the character of the government’s order was contested in an appeal concerning rights in that property.
issues.conclusion: The act of state extinguished the prior rights in the properties, and the later government order was a fresh grant; the grantees’ title had its root in that order.
issues.legal_principle: Under The Secretary of State in Council of India v. Kamachee Boye Sahaba (1859), a sovereign seizure of both private and public property is an act of state that municipal courts cannot question and leaves no prior title outstanding. The subsequent order therefore operates as a fresh grant, not as a revival of antecedent rights. The Court relied on Jijoyamba Bayi Saiba v. Kamakshi Bayi Saiba (1868), Srimant Chota Raja Saheb Mohitai v. Sundaram Ayyar (1936), and Chidambaram Chettiar v. Ramaswamy Odayar (1957), among other decisions treating the order as a grant.

rule.if: estate_property_appeal and sovereign_seizure_included_private_property and no_prior_rights_survived_seizure and later_order_returned_property

predicates.estate_property_appeal: The dispute arose in an appeal concerning rights in property whose status affected an estate-law claim.
predicates.sovereign_seizure_included_private_prope: The government, acting as a sovereign power, seized the ruler’s private property as well as public property.
predicates.no_prior_rights_survived_seizure: The seizure extinguished the prior claimants’ rights in the seized property.
predicates.later_order_returned_property: The government later issued an order returning the property to the former ruler’s family.

issues.definition: When an estate-property appeal concerns property whose prior rights were extinguished by a sovereign seizure and later returned by government order, the order creates new title as a fresh grant.

issues.legal_issue: Land shown to form part of an inam village is governed by the estate land law, and a qualifying cultivator in direct and actual possession may claim occupancy rights and a patta.
material_facts: The disputed land formed part of the Tanjore Palace Estate, whose private properties had been granted to the ruler’s widows by a government order.
Witnesses testified that the relevant land was a separate village with separate accounts, although it was included in a larger revenue vattam.
An official irrigation memoir described the relevant blocks together as a Mokhasa village and stated that the village was governed by the estate land law.
Revenue records and receipts described the village as a whole village; the land’s identity was established despite changes in its name and the absence of houses on the land.
The claimant had been in direct and actual possession of the land on the date relevant to the statutory vesting of occupancy rights.
The lower courts found the land to be part of an inam village and granted relief; the Supreme Court found that conclusion supported by the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The land was part of an inam village governed by the Madras Estates Land Act, and the claimant was entitled to occupancy rights and a patta on payment of fair rent; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 55 of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, as amended by the Third Amendment Act of 1936, a person in direct and actual possession of the land on the specified statutory date could acquire occupancy rights. The Court accepted the finding that the land formed part of a Mokhasa inam village based on witness testimony and official and revenue records, and held that the finding was supported by evidence. In describing a Mokhasa village, the Court relied on Wilson’s Glossary and Venkata Narasimha Appa Rao Bahadur v. Sobhanadri Appa Rao Bahadur (1905).

predicates.estate_land_occupancy_claim: The proceeding was a claim for occupancy rights and a patta under an estate land law.
predicates.land_was_part_of_an_inam_village: The disputed land formed part of a village held as an inam.
predicates.reliable_evidence_supported_the_land_ide: Witnesses and official or revenue records supported the identification of the disputed land as part of that village.
predicates.claimant_was_in_direct_actual_possession: The claimant was in direct and actual possession of the land at the time relevant to the statutory vesting of occupancy rights.

issues.definition: When an occupancy claim concerns land proved to be part of an inam village and the claimant was in direct and actual possession at the relevant time, the land is governed by the estate land law and the claimant is entitled to occupancy rights and a patta.
